title: Symbol Atlas
intro: The signs the corpus leans on, each with what it means, where it came from, and what it does in the notes — from the turnstile to the circled dot.

categories.logic: Connectives, quantifiers and the entailment relations.
categories.set-theory: Membership, containment and the operations on sets.
categories.algebra: Products, structure maps and the operators of algebra.
categories.analysis: Calculus, limits and the differential operators.
categories.parameters: The Greek letters the corpus uses for parameters.
categories.notation: Definitions, mappings and the glue between statements.

symbols.name: Turnstile
symbols.description: A sequent mark: what sits on the right is derivable from what sits on the left inside a formal system.
symbols.origins: From the logical notation of Peirce and the early-20th-century proof theory that followed Principia Mathematica; encoded as U+22A2 in the Unicode Mathematical Operators block (1993); TeX: \vdash.
symbols.usage: Γ ⊢ φ — an inference step of a calculus; the syntactic twin of ⊨, and the judgment behind Curry–Howard in type theory.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Double Turnstile
symbols.description: The semantic turnstile: the structure on the left makes the sentence on the right true.
symbols.origins: The double turnstile of mid-20th-century model theory, marking the syntax/semantics split it encodes; U+22A8; TeX: \models.
symbols.usage: M ⊨ φ — satisfaction; Γ ⊨ φ — semantic consequence, set against Γ ⊢ φ — syntactic derivability.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Universal Quantifier
symbols.description: Reads “for every”: the predicate that follows holds across the whole domain.
symbols.origins: The inverted A for “all”, fixed in the quantifier notation that became standard in the 1930s logic literature; U+2200; TeX: \forall.
symbols.usage: ∀x ∈ S: P(x) — definitions, axioms and invariants throughout the corpus; always paired with ∃.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Existential Quantifier
symbols.description: Reads “there is at least one”: a witness for the predicate must exist in the domain.
symbols.origins: The rotated E descends from Peirce's existential quantifier (1880s) and settled into its modern form with Peano and the 20th-century tradition; U+2203; TeX: \exists.
symbols.usage: ∃x ∈ S: P(x) — existence claims: fixed points, witnesses, separating hyperplanes.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Not Sign
symbols.description: Flips the truth of the proposition it prefixes.
symbols.origins: The typographic “not sign” of 20th-century logic, carried in ISO Latin-1 (U+00AC) before Unicode; TeX: \neg.
symbols.usage: ¬φ — negation, kept apart from the tilde ~ of informal logic and the ! of programming.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Wedge
symbols.description: Logical AND: true only when both sides are.
symbols.origins: The wedge for conjunction, standardised in the early-20th-century logical notation; U+2227; TeX: \wedge (\land).
symbols.usage: φ ∧ ψ — compound conditions; the same glyph is the meet/infimum in orders and lattices.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Vee
symbols.description: Logical OR: true when at least one side is.
symbols.origins: Companion of the wedge in the same logical-notation family; U+2228; TeX: \vee (\lor).
symbols.usage: φ ∨ ψ — alternatives and case splits; join/supremum in lattice theory.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Right Double Arrow
symbols.description: The conditional: a material “if…then” between statements.
symbols.origins: The double arrow of 20th-century logical typography, in the same family as → and ⇔; U+21D2; TeX: \implies (amsmath), \Rightarrow.
symbols.usage: P ⇒ Q — theorem statements; deliberately distinct from the function and limit arrow →.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Left Right Double Arrow
symbols.description: Both directions of implication at once: the two sides stand or fall together.
symbols.origins: The double-headed arrow for logical equivalence, standard in 20th-century texts; U+21D4; TeX: \iff (amsmath).
symbols.usage: φ ⇔ ψ — definitional equivalences and the biconditional form of a criterion.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Therefore Sign
symbols.description: Marks the concluding step: what follows has been derived.
symbols.origins: The three-dot conclusion mark of 17th-century algebraic writing, abbreviating the Latin ergo; U+2234; TeX: \therefore (amsmath).
symbols.usage: P, P ⇒ Q ∴ Q — the informal end of a derivation; its mirror is ∵ (“because”).

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Element Of
symbols.description: The membership relation: x is a member of S.
symbols.origins: Peano's ∈ (1889), standing for the Italian è, “is”; U+2208; TeX: \in.
symbols.usage: x ∈ S — membership in set theory, type signatures, and the quantifier domains ∀x ∈ S.

symbols.name: Not An Element Of
symbols.description: Membership negated: x lies outside S.
symbols.origins: The negated form of Peano's ∈; U+2209; TeX: \notin.
symbols.usage: x ∉ S — exclusions in definitions and the side conditions of theorems.

symbols.name: Subset Of
symbols.description: Containment: every member of the left set is a member of the right.
symbols.origins: The subset signs of early-20th-century set notation, in the Cantor–Peano lineage; U+2286; TeX: \subseteq.
symbols.usage: A ⊆ B — containment of sets, σ-algebras and information sets; the reflexive form of ⊂.

symbols.name: Subset Of (Proper)
symbols.description: Containment with something left over: A ⊆ B and A ≠ B.
symbols.origins: Same family as ⊆; U+2282; TeX: \subset. Publishers disagree on whether ⊂ means ⊆ or the strict relation — always say which.
symbols.usage: A ⊂ B — strict containment; check the author's convention before reading a strictness into it.

symbols.name: Union
symbols.description: Everything that is in either set.
symbols.origins: The upright cup of the set-operation notation, descended from the Cantor–Peano tradition; U+222A; TeX: \cup.
symbols.usage: A ∪ B — pooling sets; P(A ∪ B) for events, with inclusion–exclusion bridging it to ∩.

symbols.name: Intersection
symbols.description: Everything the two sets share.
symbols.origins: The inverted cup, paired with ∪ in the same notation; U+2229; TeX: \cap.
symbols.usage: A ∩ B — common elements; P(A ∩ B) for joint events, the ∧ of events.

symbols.name: Empty Set
symbols.description: The set with no members — the unique set of cardinality zero.
symbols.origins: The slashed zero ∅, popularised by the Bourbaki group's Éléments de mathématique over older forms such as Ø or { }; U+2205; TeX: \emptyset.
symbols.usage: ∅ — the impossible event P(∅) = 0, the neutral element of ∪, and the base case of constructions.

symbols.name: Multiplication Sign
symbols.description: The cross used for the ordered pairing of sets: all (a, b) with a in A and b in B.
symbols.origins: The multiplication cross of 17th-century arithmetic typography (attributed to Oughtred's Clavis Mathematicae, 1631), reused for set products; U+00D7; TeX: \times.
symbols.usage: A × B — sample spaces of joint outcomes and product spaces; kept distinct from the scalar dot ⋅ and the tensor ⊗.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Rightwards Arrow From Bar
symbols.description: Defines a function by rule: each input is sent to its output.
symbols.origins: The maplet arrow of the Bourbaki school's function notation; U+21A6; TeX: \mapsto.
symbols.usage: x ↦ f(x) — the rule itself, against the type declaration f: A → B that names it.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Circled Plus
symbols.description: Addition under a ring: the direct sum of structures, or XOR on bits.
symbols.origins: The ringed binary-operator convention that separates algebraic products from ordinary ones; U+2295; TeX: \oplus.
symbols.usage: G ⊕ H — direct sum of groups and modules; a ⊕ b — XOR in Boolean algebra and error-correcting codes.

symbols.name: Circled Times
symbols.description: The multilinear product that combines two structures into all their pairwise interactions.
symbols.origins: The ringed times of multilinear algebra, encoding a product “larger” than the ordinary one; U+2297; TeX: \otimes.
symbols.usage: V ⊗ W — tensor product of spaces; |ψ⟩ ⊗ |φ⟩ — composite quantum states; A ⊗ B — Kronecker product of matrices.

symbols.name: Circled Dot Operator
symbols.description: A ringed binary operator that writes an element-wise (Hadamard) product: two equally shaped objects multiplied slot by slot, the circle marking that the operation acts componentwise rather than being the structural product the same glyphs would name without a ring.
symbols.origins: Encoded as U+2299 in the Unicode Mathematical Operators block (Unicode 1.1, 1993) and exposed by TeX as \odot; the ringed-operator convention that separates ⊕ (direct sum), ⊗ (tensor product) and ⊙ (componentwise product) comes from 19th–20th-century algebraic typography.
symbols.usage: Element-wise multiplication in the backpropagation note — δᴸ = ∇L ⊙ σ′(zᴸ) — where ⊙ keeps the Hadamard product distinct from matrix multiplication; also the circle dot product in geometry and a modulation product in engineering.

symbols.name: Dot Operator
symbols.description: The centred dot for multiplication where × would be misread as a product of sets.
symbols.origins: U+22C5, the dot operator that displaced the middle dot · of older typography; TeX: \cdot.
symbols.usage: a ⋅ b — scalar and dot products, field multiplication; also the “per” of units, written m⋅s⁻¹.

symbols.name: Congruent To
symbols.description: Same up to relabelling: a structure-preserving bijection in both directions.
symbols.origins: U+2245; TeX: \cong; shared by algebra (isomorphism), geometry (congruence) and number theory (modular congruence).
symbols.usage: G ≅ H — groups, spaces or models that differ only in naming; ≅ says the map, not the elements, is what matters.

symbols.name: Mathematical Angle Brackets
symbols.description: Chevrons that delimit inner products, generators and tuples without the ambiguity of parentheses.
symbols.origins: The Mathematical Angle Brackets of Unicode 3.1 (2001), fixing ⟨⟩ as a pair distinct from < >; TeX: \langle, \rangle.
symbols.usage: ⟨x, y⟩ — inner products; ⟨g⟩ — the subgroup generated by g; the bra-ket ⟨ψ|φ⟩ of quantum notation uses the same family.

symbols.name: Integral Sign
symbols.description: The elongated S for summa: accumulation of a quantity over a continuum.
symbols.origins: Drawn by Leibniz (1675) for the integral of the calculus; U+222B; TeX: \int; the closed variant ∮ (U+222E) adds “around a contour”.
symbols.usage: ∫ f dx — areas, probabilities and expectations as integrals; ∮ for contour integrals in the theorems of vector calculus.

sources.label: Rudin, W. (1976). Principles of Mathematical Analysis.

symbols.name: Partial Derivative Symbol
symbols.description: Differentiation with respect to one variable while the rest are held fixed.
symbols.origins: The curly d of partial differentiation, in use among 18th–19th-century analysts (Legendre, Jacobi); U+2202; TeX: \partial.
symbols.usage: ∂f/∂x — partial derivatives and PDEs; ∂L/∂w — the gradients of the loss in the optimisation notes.

sources.label: Crowe, M. J. (1967). A History of Vector Analysis.

symbols.name: Nabla
symbols.description: The differential operator that reads a field as gradient, divergence and curl depending on how it is applied.
symbols.origins: The inverted delta used by Hamilton (1830s) for vector operations, later named “nabla” after the harp-shaped Greek instrument; U+2207; TeX: \nabla.
symbols.usage: ∇f, ∇·F, ∇×F — gradient, divergence, curl; ∇L — the gradient step of backpropagation; Δ = ∇² in physics notation.

sources.label: Crowe, M. J. (1967). A History of Vector Analysis.

symbols.name: Infinity
symbols.description: No bound: the limit that is never reached, and the size of the unbounded.
symbols.origins: The lemniscate of John Wallis (1655), from the Latin infinitas; U+221E; TeX: \infty.
symbols.usage: x → ∞ — limits and asymptotics; [−∞, ∞] — the extended reals; ∞ as the horizon of unbounded operators.

sources.label: Stillwell, J. (2010). Mathematics and Its History.

symbols.name: Proportional To
symbols.description: Two quantities that keep a fixed ratio: f = c·g for some constant c.
symbols.origins: The proportionality sign of English mathematical printing, standard in the 20th century; U+221D; TeX: \propto.
symbols.usage: F ∝ 1/r² — scaling laws and rate statements: a claim about shape only, never about scale.

sources.label: Stillwell, J. (2010). Mathematics and Its History.

symbols.name: N-Ary Summation
symbols.description: Adds a family of terms indexed over a range.
symbols.origins: Capital sigma as the summation operator, standard since Euler's century; U+2211; TeX: \sum with limits.
symbols.usage: ∑ᵢ xᵢ — means, variances, losses and series; the discrete twin of ∫.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Less-Than Or Equal To
symbols.description: Order with the boundary included: below, or exactly at.
symbols.origins: The “or equal” inequality of 20th-century printing (an older cut is ⩽); U+2264; TeX: \le.
symbols.usage: a ≤ b — bounds and constraints in optimisation, inequalities in analysis, and the ≤ of complexity upper bounds.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Greater-Than Or Equal To
symbols.description: Order with the boundary included from above.
symbols.origins: Companion of ≤ in the same printing convention; U+2265; TeX: \ge.
symbols.usage: a ≥ b — lower bounds, non-negativity constraints (λ ≥ 0) and “at least n” claims.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Not Equal To
symbols.description: The values differ.
symbols.origins: The negated equals of 20th-century typography; U+2260; TeX: \neq.
symbols.usage: a ≠ b — strict difference, kept apart from ≡ (identity) and ≈ (approximate).

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Identical To
symbols.description: Stronger than =: the same object, or the same remainder under a modulus.
symbols.origins: The triple bar of identity and congruence — Gauss's congruence notation in the Disquisitiones (1801) made ≡ standard for “same remainder mod n”; U+2261; TeX: \equiv.
symbols.usage: a ≡ b (mod n) — congruence; f ≡ g — identity of functions; definitional equality in type theory.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Almost Equal To
symbols.description: Close enough for the purpose at hand, at a stated precision.
symbols.origins: The double-waved similarity sign; U+2248; TeX: \approx.
symbols.usage: π ≈ 3.14159 — numerical values and reported estimates; distinct from ∼ (a relation between laws) and ≡ (identity).

sources.label: Rudin, W. (1976). Principles of Mathematical Analysis.

symbols.name: Tilde
symbols.description: A relation of likeness: in probability, the law a random variable follows.
symbols.origins: The tilde of similarity and distributional notation; U+223C; TeX: \sim.
symbols.usage: X ∼ N(0, 1) — the distribution of X; A ∼ B — similar figures; f ∼ g — asymptotic equivalence of functions.

symbols.name: Much Less Than
symbols.description: Not merely smaller — small enough that the leading behaviour ignores it.
symbols.origins: The doubled inequality of asymptotic comparison; U+226A; TeX: \ll.
symbols.usage: ε ≪ 1 — the regime where perturbation expansions hold; n ≫ 1 — the large-sample limit behind asymptotic arguments.

sources.label: Rudin, W. (1976). Principles of Mathematical Analysis.

symbols.name: Much Greater Than
symbols.description: Large enough that everything smaller is dropped at leading order.
symbols.origins: Counterpart of ≪ in the same asymptotic family; U+226B; TeX: \gg.
symbols.usage: N ≫ 1 — dominance in scaling arguments and the thermodynamic limit.

sources.label: Rudin, W. (1976). Principles of Mathematical Analysis.

symbols.name: Plus-Minus Sign
symbols.description: A value together with its uncertainty, or the two outcomes of a sign choice.
symbols.origins: The plus-over-minus of the French “plus ou moins”, standard for error and interval notation; U+00B1; TeX: \pm.
symbols.usage: x ± σ — measurement uncertainty and confidence intervals; (a ± b)² — both signs in the expansion.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Double-Struck E
symbols.description: The operator that averages a random quantity over its law: the probability-weighted mean.
symbols.origins: The blackboard-bold E of the double-struck operator family (Mathematical Alphanumeric Symbols, Unicode 3.1, 2001); TeX: \mathbb{E}.
symbols.usage: 𝔼[X] — expectation behind estimators, variances and risks; 𝔼[X | Y] — conditional expectation.

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

symbols.name: Up Tack
symbols.description: No coupling: in probability the joint law factorises; in geometry the directions meet at a right angle.
symbols.origins: The up tack ⊥ of geometry, reused for statistical independence and orthogonality; U+22A5; TeX: \perp.
symbols.usage: X ⊥ Y — independence (X ⊥ Y | Z conditional); v ⊥ w — perpendicular vectors; orthogonal parameters in a model.

symbols.name: Vertical Bar
symbols.description: The most overloaded glyph in the corpus: conditioning in probability, comprehension in set theory, divisibility in number theory, restriction of a map.
symbols.origins: The ASCII vertical bar (U+007C) taken over by 20th-century mathematics for “given” and “such that”; TeX: | and \mid.
symbols.usage: P(A | B) — conditioning; {x | P(x)} — set-builder; a | b — “a divides b”; f|_A — restriction of a map.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Correlation Coefficient
symbols.description: The sample linear correlation: a Latin letter by Fisher's convention, with ρ reserved for the population value.
symbols.origins: Karl Pearson's correlation coefficient (1890s), written r for the sample statistic and ρ for the parameter, under Fisher's convention that statistics take Latin letters and parameters Greek ones.
symbols.usage: r ∈ [−1, 1] — linear association in a sample; report it with the scatter it summarises, since r alone hides nonlinearity and outliers.

sources.label: Stigler, S. M. (1986). The History of Statistics.

symbols.name: Alpha
symbols.description: First Greek letter: in testing, the rate of false alarms you agree to tolerate.
symbols.origins: Greek alpha (Α), the first letter, adopted as the significance level of a test in Neyman–Pearson theory (1930s); U+03B1; TeX: \alpha.
symbols.usage: α = 0.05 — the type-I error rate; also learning rates, exponents and the fine-structure constant.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Type I and type II errors
Neyman, J., & Pearson, E. S. (1933). On the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses.

symbols.name: Beta
symbols.description: Second Greek letter: the miss rate — failing to detect an effect that is there.
symbols.origins: Greek beta (Β); the pair α/β for the two error rates arrives with the Neyman–Pearson testing framework (1930s); U+03B2; TeX: \beta.
symbols.usage: β — type-II error, with power = 1 − β; β — regression coefficients and the beta distribution.

sources.label: Wikipedia: Type I and type II errors
Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences.

symbols.name: Epsilon
symbols.description: The stand-in for an arbitrarily small positive quantity: how close is close enough.
symbols.origins: Greek epsilon (Ε); the ε–δ pair that made limits rigorous is Weierstrass's (1870s); U+03B5; TeX: \varepsilon (or \epsilon).
symbols.usage: ε > 0 — tolerances, error bounds, perturbation parameters; in numerical work, the stopping threshold.

sources.label: Rudin, W. (1976). Principles of Mathematical Analysis.

symbols.name: Delta
symbols.description: Small letter delta: an infinitesimal change, an index selector, or the error signal of a layer.
symbols.origins: Greek delta (Δ/δ), the fourth letter, used for differences since the 18th century; U+03B4; TeX: \delta.
symbols.usage: δᴸ — the backpropagation error signal; δ(x) — the Dirac delta; ε–δ limits — the small increment.

symbols.name: Capital Delta
symbols.description: A finite, measurable change — the counterpart of the infinitesimal δ.
symbols.origins: Greek capital delta (Δ), its triangular shape read as “difference”; used for finite differences since the 18th century; U+0394; TeX: \Delta.
symbols.usage: Δx — a finite increment; Δt — a time step; Δ — the Laplacian in physics notation, where mathematics writes ∇².

sources.label: Crowe, M. J. (1967). A History of Vector Analysis.

symbols.name: Theta
symbols.description: The generic unknown: the parameter a model is trying to pin down.
symbols.origins: Greek theta (Θ); Fisher's convention fixes Greek letters for parameters and Latin letters for the statistics computed from data; U+03B8; TeX: \theta.
symbols.usage: θ — the true parameter, θ̂ — its estimate, L(θ) — the likelihood over it.

sources.label: Casella, G., & Berger, R. L. (2002). Statistical Inference.

symbols.name: Mu
symbols.description: The mean of a distribution, and more generally any measure over a space.
symbols.origins: Greek mu (Μ); μ for the average and for the measure in Lebesgue's measure theory (1902); U+03BC; TeX: \mu.
symbols.usage: μ = 𝔼[X] — location of a law; μ(A) — the measure of a set; μ in units (micrometre).

symbols.name: Sigma
symbols.description: Spread of a distribution, step size of an update, and the σ that makes sets measurable.
symbols.origins: Greek sigma (Σ); σ for the standard deviation of a normal law and for the σ-algebra of measurable sets (Lebesgue); U+03C3; TeX: \sigma.
symbols.usage: σ² — variance, σ — standard deviation and SGD step size; σ-algebra — the family of sets a measure is defined on.

symbols.name: Lambda
symbols.description: Whatever scales without changing direction: an eigenvalue, a multiplier, an arrival rate.
symbols.origins: Greek lambda (Λ), the seventh letter, adopted for eigenvalues and multipliers in 19th–20th-century analysis; U+03BB; TeX: \lambda.
symbols.usage: Av = λv — eigenvalues; λ ≥ 0 — the Lagrange multiplier or the regularisation strength; λ — Poisson arrival rate.

symbols.name: Rho
symbols.description: How tightly two things move together, or how much stuff sits at a point.
symbols.origins: Greek rho (Ρ); Pearson's correlation coefficient ρ for the population value against r for the sample; U+03C1; TeX: \rho.
symbols.usage: ρ(X, Y) — the population correlation; ρ — mass or charge density; ρ(A) — the spectral radius of a matrix.

sources.label: Stigler, S. M. (1986). The History of Statistics.

symbols.name: Colon Equals
symbols.description: Introduces notation: the left side is being defined, not shown to equal the right.
symbols.origins: The := of set theory and computer science (also ≔, U+2254); TeX writes it as :=, with \coloneqq (mathtools) for the spaced form.
symbols.usage: f(x) := x² — a definition; kept distinct from = (a claim to be proved) and ≡ (identity).

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Delta Equal To
symbols.description: Definition with a triangle: the left is shorthand for the right.
symbols.origins: U+225C, the delta-equal-to of engineering and physics typography; TeX: \triangleq.
symbols.usage: A ≜ B — defining a quantity inline, common in the physics-flavoured notes where := would read as an assignment.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.

symbols.name: Rightwards Arrow
symbols.description: The workhorse arrow: a function's type, a sequence's limit, an informal implication.
symbols.origins: The right arrow of set-theoretic function notation, standard in the 20th century; U+2192; TeX: \to.
symbols.usage: f: A → B — the type of a function; xₙ → x — convergence; P → Q — informal implication, weaker in feel than ⇒.

sources.label: Cajori, F. (1928–29). A History of Mathematical Notations.
